pages.title: 1. Topological invariance of the étale topos

blocks.html: 1. Topological invariance of the étale topos

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1.1

Let \(f : X' \to X\) be a surjective, radicial, integral morphism. Then the base change functor \[ f^* : X_{\text{ét}} \to X'_{\text{ét}} \] is an equivalence of sites (i.e. an equivalence of categories which, together with any quasi-inverse functor, is continuous). Consequently the functors \[ f_* : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{X'}_{\text{ét}} \] \[ f^* : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{X'}_{\text{ét}} \] are equivalences of categories, quasi-inverse to one another.

The first assertion is well known (SGA IX 4.10 and 4.11) when \(f\) is of finite presentation or when \(f\) is flat; the general case reduces to the one where \(f\) is of finite presentation. Indeed, we already know that the functor \(f^*\) is fully faithful (SGA 1 IX 3.4). It suffices to prove that \(f^*\) is essentially surjective, i.e. that every \(Z'\) étale over \(X'\) "comes from" a \(Z\) étale over \(X\). Using the fact that \(f\) is a universal homeomorphism, together with the full faithfulness of \(f^*\), we are reduced to the case where \(X\), \(X'\), \(Z'\) are affine, spectra of rings \(A\), \(A'\), \(B'\). Writing \(A'\) as the inductive limit of its finite-type sub-\(A\)-algebras \(A'_i\), \(B'\) comes from an étale algebra \(B'_i\) over some \(A'_i\) (cf. EGA IV 8), which reduces us to the case where \(A'\) is integral and of finite type over \(A\), hence finite over \(A\). We then have an \(A\)-isomorphism \(A' \simeq A''/J\), where \(A'' \simeq A[t_1, \ldots t_n]\) and \(J\) is an ideal of \(A''\). Writing \(J\) as the inductive limit of its finite-type sub-ideals \(J_i\), and setting \(A'_i = A''/J_i\), we again have \(A' = \varinjlim_i A'_i\), so \(B'\) comes from an étale algebra \(B'_i\) over some \(A'_i\) (loc. cit.). On the other hand, since \(\operatorname{Spec} A' \to \operatorname{Spec} A\) is surjective, so is \(\operatorname{Spec} A'_i \to \operatorname{Spec} A\), and moreover one checks easily that, since \(\operatorname{Spec} A' \to \operatorname{Spec} A\) is radicial, so is \(\operatorname{Spec} A'_i \to \operatorname{Spec} A\) for \(i\) large enough (apply EGA IV 1.9.9 to \(\operatorname{Spec} A\)(∗)). This reduces us to the case where \(A'\) is one of the \(A'_i\), hence of finite presentation over \(A\).
This proves the first assertion of 2.1. The fact that \(f_*\) and \(f^*\) are quasi-inverse equivalences of one another follows at once.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.2

Let \(F\) be an abelian sheaf on \(X\), \(F'\) its inverse image on \(X'\); then the canonical homomorphisms \[ (*) \qquad H^i(X,F) \to H^i(X',F') \] are isomorphisms. Likewise, if \(F'\) is an abelian sheaf on \(X'\) and \(F\) its image on \(X\), the canonical homomorphisms \((*)\) are isomorphisms.
Examples 1.3
Here are some frequently occurring examples of applications of 1.1:
a) \(X'\) is a subscheme of \(X\) having the same underlying set as \(X\), i.e. defined by a nil-ideal \(I\).
b) \(X\) is a scheme over a separably closed field \(k\), \(k'\) is an algebraic closure of \(k\), and \(X' = X \otimes_k k'\).

c) Let \(X\) be a geometrically unibranch scheme (for example an algebraic curve over a field \(k\) whose only singularities are "cuspidal" singularities, excluding in particular ordinary double points). Then, if \(X'\) is the normalization of \(X_{\text{red}}\), by definition \(X' \to X\) is radicial, so 2.1 applies.
Remarks 1.4

A morphism \(f\) as in 1.1 is a universal homeomorphism, i.e. it is a homeomorphism and remains one under any base extension of the base. Conversely, if \(f\) is a universal homeomorphism, one proves that \(f\) satisfies the hypotheses of 2.1 (∗), which explains the title of the present section.

Let us point out explicitly, in connection with example 2.3 c), that if \(X\) is an algebraic curve (over an algebraically closed field \(k\), to fix ideas) having at least one singular point that is not "unibranch" (for example an ordinary double point), then (with \(X'\) denoting the normalization of \(X_{\text{red}}\)) the conclusion of 2.2 already fails for \(H^1\) and constant coefficients (compare SGA 1 I 11 a) and SGA 1 IX 5).

footnotes.html: (∗) Let \(S_i \subset \operatorname{Spec} A\) be the set of \(s \in S\) such that the fibre of \(X_i = \operatorname{Spec} A'_i\) at \(s\) is of separable rank 1. Then the \(S_i\) are constructible subsets of \(S\) (EGA IV 9.7.9) forming an increasing family, whose union is \(S\) by the hypothesis on \(S' = \operatorname{Spec} A' \to S\) and the fact that the fibres of \(S'_i\) are noetherian schemes. Hence \(S = S_i\) for \(i\) large enough, by EGA IV 1.9.9, q.e.d.
(∗) Cf. EGA IV 8.11.6 if \(f\) is of finite presentation, and EGA IV 18.12.11 in the general case.

pages.title: 2. Sheaves on the spectrum of a field

blocks.html: 2. Sheaves on the spectrum of a field

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.1

Let \(k\) be a field, \(\bar{k}\) a separable closure of \(k\), \(\pi = \operatorname{Gal}(\bar{k}/k)\) its topological Galois group, \(X = \operatorname{Spec} k\), \(\overline{X} = \operatorname{Spec} \bar{k}\) (on which \(\pi\) acts on the left). Consider the canonical functor \[ i : X_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \] (defined by \(i(X')(X'') = \operatorname{Hom}_X(X',X'')\)), and the canonical functor \[ j : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \mathscr{B}_\pi \] from the category of sheaves on \(X_{\text{ét}}\) to the category \(\mathscr{B}_\pi\) (cf. IV 2.7) of (discrete) sets on which \(\pi\) acts continuously on the left, defined by \[ j(F) = \varinjlim_\alpha F(\operatorname{Spec} k_\alpha) , \] where \(k_\alpha\) ranges over the finite sub-extensions of \(\bar{k}\). Then \(i\) and \(j\) are equivalences of categories. (Consequently, the topos \(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\) is equivalent (IV 3.4) to the "classifying topos" \(\mathscr{B}_\pi\).)

The composite functor \[ ji: X_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to (\pi\text{-Ens}) \] is an equivalence of categories, by the fundamental theorem of Galois theory (in the form of SGA 1 V). Since \(\mathscr{B}_\pi\) is obviously a topos (II 4.14), the same holds for \(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\). Moreover, a family \((X_i \to X)\) of morphisms in \(X_{\text{ét}}\) is covering if and only if it is surjective, i.e. its image in \(\mathscr{B}_\pi\) is surjective, or equivalently, covering for the canonical topology of \(\mathscr{B}_\pi\), which shows that the topology of \(X_{\text{ét}}\) is indeed its canonical topology. Consequently \(i\) is an equivalence, and hence so is \(j\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.2

The functor \(j\) of 2.1 induces an equivalence between the category of abelian sheaves on \(X = \operatorname{Spec} k\) and the category of Galois \(\pi\)-modules.
Indeed, the latter are precisely the "abelian groups" of the topos \(\mathscr{B}_\pi\). One sees likewise, by "transport of structure":

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3

Let \(F\) be an abelian sheaf on \(X = \operatorname{Spec} k\), and \(M = j(F)\) the associated Galois \(\pi\)-module; then one has a canonical isomorphism of \(\partial\)-functors in \(F\): \[ H^*(X,F) \simeq H^*(\pi,M) , \] (where the right-hand side denotes Galois cohomology, studied for example in Serre's course C.G.).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.4

Suppose \(k\) is separably closed. Then the functor \[ \Gamma : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to (\mathrm{Ens}) \] is an equivalence of categories. If \(F\) is an abelian sheaf on \(X = \operatorname{Spec} k\), then \(H^i(X,F) = 0\) for \(i \neq 0\). (In other words, the topos \(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\) is a "punctual topos" (IV 2.2).)

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.5

Let \(k'\) be a separably closed extension of a separably closed field \(k\), \(X = \operatorname{Spec} k\), \(X' = \operatorname{Spec} k'\), \(u : X' \to X\) the canonical morphism. Then the functor \[ u^* : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{X'}_{\text{ét}} \] is an equivalence of categories.

pages.title: 3. Fibre functors relative to the geometric points of a scheme

blocks.html: 3. Fibre functors relative to the geometric points of a scheme

Let \(X\) be a scheme. We shall call a geometric point of \(X\) any \(X\)-scheme \(\xi\) that is the spectrum of a separably closed field \(\Omega\). Giving such a point is thus equivalent to giving an ordinary point \(x \in X\) together with a separably closed extension \(\Omega\) of the residue field \(k(x)\) of \(X\). The most frequent case for us will be the one where \(\Omega\) is a separable closure of \(k(x)\), which we shall then generally denote by \(\overline{k(x)}\), the corresponding geometric point of \(X\) being then denoted \(\bar{x}\). For given \(x \in X\), the \(\overline{k(x)}\) (resp. \(\bar{x}\)) are determined up to a non-unique \(k\)-isomorphism (resp. \(X\)-isomorphism).
Remarks 3.2

In most geometric questions, it is more natural to restrict to the case where \(\Omega\) is algebraically closed. The different convention used here is specific to the study of the étale topology. It is the convention we had adopted in the definition of the fundamental group SGA 1 V 7. But one should note that the developments of loc. cit. are equally valid with the convention adopted here (for the property of \(\Omega\) used there is that every étale covering of the spectrum of \(\Omega\) is trivial, i.e. precisely that \(\Omega\) is separably closed).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3.3

Let \(X\) be a scheme, \(\xi\) a geometric point of \(X\), \(u : \xi \to X\) its structural morphism. We call the (geometric) fibre functor relative to \(\xi\), and denote by \(F \mapsto F_\xi\), the functor \[ \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to (\mathrm{Ens}) \] composed of \[ \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \xrightarrow{\ u^*\ } \widetilde{\xi}_{\text{ét}} \xrightarrow{\ \Gamma_\xi\ } (\mathrm{Ens}) . \]

One may also say that, thanks to 2.4, a geometric point \(\xi\) of \(X\) defines a point of the topos \(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\) (IV 6.1), of which one simply takes the associated fibre functor (loc. cit.).

Since the functor \(\Gamma_\xi\) (the functor of sections over \(\xi\)) is an equivalence of categories (12.4), knowledge of the fibre functors \(F \mapsto F_\xi\) is essentially equivalent to that of the inverse-image functors \(u^*\). Let us note, moreover, that it follows at once from 2.5 that if \(\xi\) is a geometric point of \(X\) such that there exists an \(X\)-morphism \(\xi' \to \xi\) (i.e. \(\xi'\) corresponds to a separably closed extension \(\Omega'\) of \(\Omega\)), then the canonical homomorphism \(F_\xi \to F_{\xi'}\) is a functorial isomorphism \[ F_\xi \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F_{\xi'} . \] This shows that, for the study of fibre functors, one may (at the cost of replacing \(\Omega\) by the separable algebraic closure of \(k\) in \(\Omega\)) restrict to the case where \(\Omega = k(\xi)\) is a separable closure \(\overline{k(x)}\) of \(k(x)\), and that the fibre functors corresponding to the geometric points of \(X\) localized at the same \(x \in X\) are isomorphic to one another (in a non-unique way).
In accordance with the conventions of 3.1, we shall denote by \(F_{\bar{x}}\) a fibre functor corresponding to the choice of a separable closure \(\overline{k(x)}\) of \(k(x)\).

Let us point out an obvious transitivity property (which shows the technical usefulness of not restricting exclusively to geometric points defined by separable closures of residue fields): Let \(f = X' \to X\) be a morphism of schemes and \(u' : \xi' \to X'\) a geometric point of \(X'\); then \(u = f u' : \xi' \to X\) is a geometric point of \(X\), which we shall denote by \(\xi\); relative to these geometric points one has an isomorphism, functorial in \(F \in \mathrm{Ob}\, \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\): \[ f^*(F)_{\xi'} \simeq F_\xi . \] This indeed follows from the transitivity formula for inverse-image functors \[ (fu)^* \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } u^* f^* . \]

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.5

Let \(X\) be a scheme.

a) For every geometric point \(\xi\) of \(X\), the fibre functor \(F \mapsto F_\xi : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) commutes with arbitrary \(\varinjlim\) (indexed by categories \(\in \mathcal{U}\)) and with finite \(\varprojlim\) (∗). In particular, it transforms sheaves of groups (resp. abelian sheaves, etc...) into groups (resp. abelian groups, etc...).

b) As \(x\) ranges over the points of \(X\), the fibre functors \(F_{\bar{x}}\) form a "conservative" family of functors, i.e. if \(u : F \to G\) is a homomorphism of sheaves on \(X\), then \(u\) is an isomorphism if and only if, for every \(x \in X\), the corresponding homomorphism \(u_{\bar{x}} : F_{\bar{x}} \to G_{\bar{x}}\) is one (∗∗).
Let us note immediately, in view of the exactness properties of a), the following formal consequences of b):

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.6

Let \(u : F \to G\) be a homomorphism of sheaves. Then \(u\) is a monomorphism (resp. an epimorphism) if and only if, for every \(x \in X\), \(u_{\bar{x}} : F_{\bar{x}} \to G_{\bar{x}}\) is injective (resp. surjective).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.7

Let \(u, v : F \to G\) be two morphisms of sheaves on \(X\); then \(u = v\) if and only if, for every \(x \in X\), one has \(u_{\bar{x}} = v_{\bar{x}} : F_{\bar{x}} \to G_{\bar{x}}\). In particular, if \(u,v\) are two sections of \(F\), then \(u = v\) if and only if \(u_{\bar{x}} = v_{\bar{x}}\) in \(F_{\bar{x}}\) for every \(x \in X\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.8

Let \(F \to G \to H\) be a sequence of two homomorphisms of sheaves on \(X\); then the sequence is exact if and only if for every \(x \in X\), the corresponding sequence \(F_{\bar{x}} \to G_{\bar{x}} \to H_{\bar{x}}\) is exact.
We leave it to the reader to deduce the corollaries(∗), which will moreover be partially proved in the proof that follows.

Assertion a) follows from the exactness properties already pointed out in (VII 1.4) for every inverse-image functor, such as \(u^* : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \widetilde{\xi}_{\text{ét}}\), and from the fact that \(\widetilde{\xi}_{\text{ét}} \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) is an equivalence. To prove b), we note the following formula, which gives a procedure for computing the fibre functors:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.9(∗∗)

Let \(\xi \xrightarrow{\ u\ } X\) be a geometric point of \(X\), and let \(C_\xi\) be the category of "étale \(X\)-schemes that are \(\xi\)-pointed", i.e. of pairs \((X', u')\), where \(X' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}}\) is a scheme étale over \(X\), and \(u'\) is an \(X\)-morphism \(\xi \to X'\). Then the opposite category \(C_\xi^o\) is filtered and for a variable sheaf \(F\) (resp. presheaf \(P\)) on \(X\), one has a canonical functorial isomorphism \[ F_\xi \simeq \varinjlim_{C_\xi^o} F(X'), \qquad (\text{resp. } (aP)_\xi \simeq \varinjlim_{C_\xi^o} P(X') ), \] (where \(aP = \) the sheaf associated to \(P\)).

Indeed, let us first note that for every presheaf \(P\) on \(\xi_{\text{ét}}\), if \(aP\) is the associated sheaf, the natural homomorphism \[ P(\xi) \to aP(\xi) \] is an isomorphism, as follows at once, for example, from the explicit computation of \(aP\) as \(L(LP)\) (II 3.19.). Let \(\varphi : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{\xi}_{\text{ét}}\) be the "inverse image" functor; then \(u^* = \varphi^*\) is none other (III 2.3.(d)) than the composite \(a\, \varphi'\, i\), where \(i : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \widehat{X}_{\text{ét}}\) is the inclusion functor, and \(a : \widehat{\xi}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{\xi}_{\text{ét}}\) is the "associated sheaf" functor. By the preceding remark we find \[ u^*(F)(\xi) = (\varphi'i(F))(\xi) , \] so that it suffices to apply the explicit expression for \(\varphi'\) given in the proof of . The resp. case, where one starts with a presheaf \(P\) on \(X\), is proved likewise, using the functorial isomorphism \(\varphi^*a(P) \simeq a \varphi(P)\) . The fact that the category \(C_\xi\) is filtered (which remains valid for any \(X\)-scheme \(\xi\), not necessarily reduced to a geometric point) follows at once from the fact that in \(C_\xi\) finite projective limits exist, which in turn follows from the fact that \(X_{\text{ét}}\) is a subcategory of \((\mathrm{Sch})_{/X}\) stable under finite projective limits.

Now let \(u : F \to G\) be a homomorphism of sheaves on \(X\) such that, for every \(x \in X\), \(u_{\bar{x}} : F_{\bar{x}} \to G_{\bar{x}}\) is a monomorphism; let us prove that \(u\) is a monomorphism. For this, we must prove that if \(X' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}}\) and \(\varphi, \psi \in F(X')\) are such that \(u(\varphi) = u(\psi)\), then \(\varphi = \psi\). Replacing \(X\) by \(X'\) and using the transitivity of fibre functors, we may assume \(X = X'\). For every \(x \in X\), we have \(u(\varphi)_{\bar{x}} = u(\psi)_{\bar{x}}\), i.e. \(u_{\bar{x}}(\varphi_{\bar{x}}) = u_{\bar{x}}(\psi_{\bar{x}})\), hence \(\varphi_{\bar{x}} = \psi_{\bar{x}}\) since \(u_{\bar{x}}\) is a monomorphism. Using 3.9, it follows that there exists \(X'_x \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}}\), whose image contains \(x\), such that \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) have the same inverse image on \(X'_x\). Since, as \(x\) varies in \(X\), the \(X'_x\) form a covering family of \(X\), it follows that \(\varphi = \psi\).

This proves that if the \(u_{\bar{x}}\) are monomorphisms, so is \(u\). Suppose moreover that the \(u_{\bar{x}}\) are epimorphisms; let us prove that so is \(u\), and hence that \(u\) is an isomorphism. It remains to prove that for every \(X' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}}\) and every \(\psi \in G(X')\), there exists \(\varphi \in F(X')\) such that \(u(X')(\varphi) = \psi\). We may again assume \(X'=X\), and using 3.9 we see that for every \(x \in X\), there exists \(X'_x \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}}\) such that the image of \(X'_x\) in \(X\) contains \(x\), together with a \(\varphi_x \in F(X'_x)\) whose image in \(G(X'_x)\) is the inverse image of \(\psi\). Using the fact that \(u\) is a monomorphism, we see that the \(\varphi_x\) coincide on the \(X'_x \times_X X'_y\) (\(x,y \in X\)), and hence come from a well-determined \(\varphi \in F(X)\), and we then have \(u(\varphi) = \psi\), since the inverse images on the \(X'_x\) coincide. q.e.d.

blocks.title: Scholium
blocks.html:
Scholium 3.10

Theorem 3.5 implies that the collection of "fibre functors" for the étale topology enjoys the same essential properties as in the usual theory of sheaves on a topological space. We shall use 3.5 and its corollaries very frequently, and for this reason we shall generally dispense with referring to them explicitly.

For every \(x \in X\) we shall also denote, by abuse of language, by \(x\) the \(X\)-scheme \(\operatorname{Spec} k(x)\), with the usual structural morphism \[ i_x : x = \operatorname{Spec} k(x) \to X . \] It gives rise to a canonical functor \[ i_x^* : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{x}_{\text{ét}} . \] If \(F\) is a sheaf on \(X\), we set \(F_x = i_x^*(F)\); this is thus a sheaf on \(x = \operatorname{Spec} k(x)\) (and as such may also be identified with a scheme étale over \(x\), by virtue of 2.1). It depends functorially on \(F\), and the functor \(i_x^* : F \mapsto F_x\) again commutes with arbitrary \(\varinjlim\) and finite \(\varprojlim\), by virtue of VII 1.4.

If \(\bar{x} = \operatorname{Spec} \overline{k(x)}\), the fibre functor \(F \mapsto F_{\bar{x}}\) is canonically isomorphic to the composite of the functor \(F \mapsto F_x\) and the functor \(j\) of 1.1 (taking into account that the latter is isomorphic to the fibre functor relative to the geometric point \(\operatorname{Spec} \bar{k}\) of \(\operatorname{Spec} k\)). It follows at once from this and from 3.5 that the system of functors \((F \mapsto F_x)\) (\(x \in X\)) is again conservative. Moreover, if \(k(x)\) is separably closed, i.e. \(x = \bar{x}\), the notations \(F_x\) and \(F_{\bar{x}}\) are, strictly speaking, contradictory (the first denoting an object of \(\widetilde{x}_{\text{ét}}\), the second a set), but by virtue of 1.1 this is an inessential contradiction.

It follows from the preceding remarks that if \(\bar{x} = \operatorname{Spec} \overline{k(x)}\), then for every sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the group \(\pi_x = \operatorname{Gal}(\overline{k(x)}/k(x))\) acts naturally (on the left) on the fibre set \(F_{\bar{x}}\), so that \(F \mapsto F_{\bar{x}}\) may in fact be regarded as a functor \[ \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \mathscr{B}_{\pi_x} \] knowledge of which is essentially equivalent (thanks to 1.1) to that of the functor \(F \mapsto F_x\).

This shows, in an important special case, that contrary to what happens in the case of sheaves on topological spaces, the "fibre functors" in general admit non-trivial automorphisms. More generally, we shall determine in 7.9 all the homomorphisms from one fibre functor to another.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 3.13

Here is a sometimes useful generalization of 3.5 b). Consider a subset \(E\) of \(X\) such that for every étale morphism \(f : X' \to X\), \(E' = f^{-1}(E)\) is "very dense" in \(X'\) (EGA IV 10.1.3), i.e. such that for every \(f\) as above, every open set \(U\) of \(X'\) containing \(E'\) is equal to \(X'\). Then the fibre functors \(F_{\bar{x}}\) on \(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\), for \(x \in E\), already form a "conservative family" (and consequently corollaries 3.6, 3.7 and 3.8 remain valid when one restricts to choosing \(x \in E\) there). This is seen immediately by revisiting the proof given of 3.5 b). The preceding result applies in particular in the following situations:

a) \(X\) is a Jacobson scheme (EGA IV 10.4.1.), for example locally of finite type over a field, or over \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbf{Z})\), and \(E\) is the set of closed points of \(X\).

b) \(X\) is locally of finite type over a scheme \(S\), and \(E\) is the set of points of \(X\) that are closed in their fibre.

c) \(X\) is locally noetherian, and \(E\) is the set of \(x \in X\) such that \(\bar{x}\) is a finite set (i.e. a semi-local scheme of dimension \(\leqslant 1\)) cf. EGA IV 10.5.3 and 10.5.5.

footnotes.html: (∗) It is thus indeed a "fibre functor" in the sense of Exp. IV.
(∗∗) There are thus "enough fibre functors" of the form \(F \mapsto F_{\bar{x}}\), in the terminology of IV 6.5.

blocks.html: 4. Strictly local rings and schemes
Let us recall that, following Azumaya, a local ring \(A\) is said to be henselian if it satisfies the following equivalent conditions:

(i) Every algebra \(B\) finite over \(A\) is a direct product \(\prod_i B_i\) of local rings (the \(B_i\) are then necessarily isomorphic to the \(B_{\mathfrak{m}_i}\), where \(\mathfrak{m}_i\) ranges over the maximal ideals of \(B\)).

(ii) Every algebra \(B\) over \(A\) that is a localization of a finite-type algebra \(C\) over \(A\) at a prime ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\) lying over the maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{M}\) of \(A\), and such that \(B/\mathfrak{M}B\) is finite over \(k = A/\mathfrak{M}\), is finite over \(A\).
(iii) As (ii), but assuming \(C\) étale over \(A\) at \(\mathfrak{p}\) and \(k \to B/\mathfrak{M}B\) an isomorphism.

(iv) "Hensel's lemma" in its classical form holds for \(A\), i.e. for every monic polynomial \(F \in A[T]\), denoting by \(\dot{F} \in k[T]\) the corresponding reduced polynomial, and for every decomposition \[ \dot{F} = \dot{F}_1 \dot{F}_2 \] of \(\dot{F}\) into a product of two coprime monic polynomials, \(\dot{F}_1\) and \(\dot{F}_2\) lift (necessarily uniquely) to \(F_1, F_2 \in A[T]\), such that \(F = F_1 F_2\).

For the proof of these equivalences and the general properties of henselian rings, cf. EGA IV 18.5.11. Let us recall that if \(A\) is an arbitrary local ring, one shows (Nagata) that one can find a local homomorphism, \[ A \to A^h \] with \(A^h\) henselian, which is universal for the local homomorphisms from \(A\) into noetherian local rings. The ring \(A^h\) is called the henselization of \(A\). The construction given in EGA IV 18.6 (different from that of Nagata) consists in setting \[ A^h = \varinjlim_i A_i , \] where \(A_i\) ranges over the \(A\)-algebras that are essentially of finite type and essentially étale over \(A\) (i.e. localizations of an étale algebra over \(A\)) such that \(A \to A_i\) is a local homomorphism and the residue extension \(k(A_i)/k(A)\) is trivial. This construction shows in particular that \(A^h\) is flat over \(A\) and that if \(A\) is noetherian, so is its henselian closure.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.2

A local ring \(A\) is said to be strictly local if it satisfies one of the following equivalent conditions:

(i) \(A\) is henselian (4.1) and its residue field is separably closed.

(ii) Every local homomorphism \(A \to B\), where \(B\) is a localization of an étale algebra over \(A\), is an isomorphism.

A scheme is called a strictly local scheme if it is isomorphic to the spectrum of a strictly local ring.

The equivalence of (i) and (ii) follows at once from 4.1. Note that, in geometric form, 4.2 (ii) (resp. 4.1 (iii)) can be expressed by saying that for every scheme \(X\) étale over \(Y = \operatorname{Spec} A\), and every point \(x\) of the fibre \(X_y\) (respectively every point of \(X_y\) rational over \(k(y)\)), where \(y\) is the closed point of \(Y\), there exists a section of \(X\) over \(Y\) passing through \(y\) (a section that is, moreover, necessarily unique).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.3

Let \(X\) be a scheme, \(\mathcal{O}_{X_{\text{ét}}}\) the sheaf on \(X_{\text{ét}}\) defined by \[ \mathcal{O}_{X_{\text{ét}}}(X') = \Gamma(X', \mathcal{O}_{X'}) \] (compare VII 2. c) ), \(u : \xi = \operatorname{Spec}(\Omega) \to X\) a geometric point of \(X\). We call the strictly local ring of \(X\) at \(\xi\), and denote by \(\mathcal{O}_{X,\xi}\), or simply \(\mathcal{O}_\xi\), the stalk of the sheaf \(\mathcal{O}_{X_{\text{ét}}}\) at the point \(\xi\). Its spectrum is called the strict localization of \(X\) at \(\xi\).

By virtue of 3.9, one has the following description of the stalk \(\mathcal{O}_{X,\xi}\): \[ (*) \qquad \mathcal{O}_{X,\xi} = \varinjlim \Gamma(X', \mathcal{O}_{X'}) , \] where \(X'\) ranges over the opposite filtered category of the category of schemes étale over \(X\) that are \(\xi\)-pointed, i.e. equipped with an \(X\)-morphism \(\xi \to X'\). By the transitivity of inductive limits, one may replace \(\Gamma(X', \mathcal{O}_{X'})\) on the right-hand side by \(\mathcal{O}_{X',x'}\), where \(x'\) is the image of \(\xi\) in \(X'\), and one obtains the expression \[ (**) \qquad \mathcal{O}_{X,\xi} = \varinjlim_i A_i \] where \(A_i\) ranges over the algebras that are essentially of finite type and étale over \(A = \mathcal{O}_{X,x}\), equipped with a \(k\)-homomorphism \(k(A_i) \to \Omega\). (N.B. \(x\) denotes the image of \(\xi\) in \(X\)). Of course, the transition homomorphisms between the \(A_i\) are the local homomorphisms of \(A\)-algebras \(A_i \to A_j\) that make the corresponding triangle \[ \xymatrix{ k(A_i) \ar[r] \ar[dr] & k(A_j) \ar[d] \\ & \Omega } \] commute, which implies that if there exists an admissible homomorphism from \(A_i\) to \(A_j\), the latter is unique. Hence the inductive limit \((**)\) is a limit relative to a filtered, increasing, ordered index set.

The description \((**)\) shows that the strict local ring of \(X\) at \(\xi\) depends essentially only on the usual local ring \(A = \mathcal{O}_{X,x}\) (\(x=u(\xi)\)), and on the extension \(\Omega\) of \(k = k(A)\). It is also called the strict henselization of \(A\) (relative to the separably closed extension \(\Omega\) of \(k\) under consideration) and will be denoted \(A^{hs}\). We refer to EGA IV 18.8 for the general properties of \(A^{hs}\). Let us simply note that the given construction shows again that \(A^{hs}\) is flat over \(A\), and that it is noetherian if \(A\) is. On the other hand, one easily shows (loc. cit.) that the local homomorphism \[ A \to A^{hs} \] equipped with the \(k\)-homomorphism \[ k(A^{hs}) \to \Omega \] is a solution of the universal problem, relative to the data of \(A\) and of the extension \(\Omega\) of \(k\), corresponding to the search for local homomorphisms \[ A \to A' , \] with \(A'\) strictly local, equipped with a \(k\)-homomorphism \[ k(A') \to \Omega . \] In particular, \(A^{hs}\) is indeed a strictly local ring (which justifies the terminology of 4.3).

Let us keep the notations of 4.3 and choose an affine open neighbourhood \(U\) of \(x\). Note that in 3.9 one may obviously restrict to those \(X'\) that are affine over \(U\). These then form a pseudo-filtered projective system of affine schemes, so that we are in the general situation of VII 5 (cf. VII 5.12 b). By virtue of the expression \((*)\) for \(\mathcal{O}_{X,\xi}\), one has an \(X\)-isomorphism \[ (***) \qquad \varprojlim_{\substack{X'\ \text{étale} \\ \text{affine over } U, \\ X'\ \xi\text{-pointed}}} X' \simeq \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,\xi} \] which makes precise the intuitive geometric meaning of \(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{X,\xi})\) as the "limit of the étale neighbourhoods of \(\xi\)".

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.6

Let \(X\) be a strictly local scheme, \(x\) its closed point, which is thus a geometric point of \(X\). Then the functor \(F \mapsto \Gamma(X,F) : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) is canonically isomorphic to the fibre functor \(F \mapsto F_x\), and consequently commutes with arbitrary \(\varinjlim\) (∗).

Indeed, by virtue of def. 4.2 (ii), the final object \(X\) of the category of \(X'\) étale and \(x\)-pointed over \(X\) considered in 3.9 dominates all the other objects, so \(\varinjlim F(X')\) is canonically isomorphic to \(F(X)\), q.e.d.
In particular, the functor induced by \(\Gamma\) on the category of abelian sheaves is exact, so we conclude

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.7

Under the conditions of 4.6, one has, for every abelian sheaf \(F\) on \(X\): \[ H^q(X,F) = 0 \quad \text{for } q \neq 0 . \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.8

Let \(X\) be a scheme, \(\xi\) a geometric point of \(X\), \(\overline{X} = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,x}\) the corresponding strict localization scheme, \(F\) a variable sheaf on \(X\), \(\overline{F}\) its inverse image on \(\overline{X}\); then one has a functorial isomorphism \[ F_\xi \simeq \Gamma(\overline{X},\overline{F}) . \]
Indeed, \(\xi\) may be regarded as a geometric point of \(\overline{X}\) as well, and it suffices to apply 4.6 and the transitivity of fibres (3.4).

pages.title: 5. Application to the computation of the stalks of the \(R^q f_*\)

blocks.html: 5. Application to the computation of the stalks of the \(R^q f_*\)

Let \[ f : X \to Y \] be a morphism of schemes and \(F\) an abelian sheaf on \(X\); we propose to determine the \(R^q f_*(F)\). By virtue of 3.5, it amounts, up to minor details, to knowing the geometric stalks \(R^q f_*(F)_{\bar{y}}\), for \(y \in Y\). Now (V 5.1) \(R^q f_*(F)\) is the sheaf associated to the presheaf \[ \mathscr{H}^q : Y' \mapsto H^q(X \times_Y Y', F) \] on \(Y\), and consequently (3.9) \[ R^q f_*(F)_{\bar{y}} = \varinjlim_{Y'} \mathscr{H}^q(Y'), \] where the inductive limit is taken over the opposite filtered category of the category of \(Y'\) étale over \(Y\) pointed by \(\bar{y}\). Choosing an affine open neighbourhood \(U\) of \(y\), one may restrict, in the limit on the right-hand side, to the cofinal category of those \(Y'\) that are affine and over \(U\). One thus obtains \[ (5.1.1) \qquad R^q f_*(F)_{\bar{y}} \simeq \varinjlim H^q(X \times_Y Y', F), \] where \(Y'\) varies in the preceding category. Let us introduce \[ \overline{Y} = \operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{Y,\bar{y}}) = \varprojlim Y' \] (cf 4.5), and \[ \overline{X} = X \times_Y \overline{Y} . \]

Note that in the projective system of the \(X \times_Y Y'\) (deduced from that of the \(Y'\) by the base change \(X \to Y\)), the transition morphisms are affine; we are thus in the general conditions of VII 5.1, and one sees at once, from the construction of \(\varprojlim\) in loc. cit., that one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \overline{X} = \varprojlim X \times_Y Y' . \] Let us denote by \(\overline{F}\) the sheaf on \(\overline{X}\) that is the inverse image of \(F\); then one obtains a canonical homomorphism \[ \varinjlim_{Y'} H^q(X \times_Y Y', F) \to H^q(\overline{X},\overline{F}) \] whence, comparing with 5.1.1, a canonical homomorphism \[ (5.1.2) \qquad R^q f_*(F)_{\bar{y}} \to H^q(\overline{X},\overline{F}), \] obviously functorial in \(F\).

Now suppose \(f : X \to Y\) is quasi-compact and quasi-separated; then so is \(X' \times_Y Y' \to Y'\), and since \(Y'\) is affine, the \(X \times_Y Y'\) are quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Using (5.1.1) and the passage-to-the-limit theorem VII 5.8, one then obtains:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 5.2

Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphism of schemes, \(F\) an abelian sheaf on \(X\), \(y\) a point of \(Y\), \(\bar{y}\) the geometric point above \(y\), relative to a separable closure \(k(\bar{y})\) of \(k(y)\), \(\overline{Y} = \operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{O}_{Y,\bar{y}})\) the corresponding strict localization scheme, \(\overline{X} = X \times_Y \overline{Y}\), \(\overline{F}\) the inverse image of \(F\) on \(\overline{X}\). Then the canonical homomorphism (5.1.2) is an isomorphism: \[ R^q f_*(F)_{\bar{y}} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(\overline{X},\overline{F}) . \]

This statement practically reduces the determination of the stalks of a sheaf \(R^q f_*(F)\) to the determination of the cohomology of a prescheme over a strictly local scheme, and will be constantly used in what follows. Technically, it is 5.2 that explains the important role of the henselian rings and strictly local rings in the study of étale cohomology.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.3

The statement remains valid for \(R^0 f_*(F) = f_*(F)\), for an arbitrary sheaf of sets. On the other hand, 5.2 also remains valid for \(R^1 f_*(F)\), when \(F\) is a sheaf of groups (not necessarily commutative), taking the usual definition of \(R^1 f_*(F)\) (cf. Giraud's thesis).

Now suppose that \(f\) is a finite morphism. Then \(\bar{f} : \overline{X} \to \overline{Y}\) is a finite morphism, and since \(\overline{Y}\) is strictly local, it follows that \(\overline{X}\) is a finite sum of strictly local schemes \(\overline{X}_i\). Consequently, using 4.7 we find \[ (5.4.1) \qquad H^q(\overline{X},\overline{F}) = 0 \quad \text{for } q \neq 0 . \] On the other hand, note that the components \(\overline{X}_i\) of \(\overline{X}\) correspond to the points \(\bar{x}_i\) of \(\overline{X}\) above the closed point \(\bar{y}\) of \(\overline{Y}\), i.e. to the points of \(\overline{X}_{\bar{y}} = X_y \otimes_{k(y)} k(\bar{y})\). Moreover, these points may be regarded as geometric points of \(X\), and \(\overline{X}_i\) is then none other than the strict localization scheme of \(X\) at \(\bar{x}_i\). One thus has (4.8) \[ H^0(\overline{X}_i,\overline{F}) \simeq F_{\bar{x}_i} , \] whence \[ (5.4.2) \qquad H^0(\overline{X},\overline{F}) = \prod_i F_{\bar{x}_i} , \] which is a functorial isomorphism in the sheaf of sets \(F\) (there is no need here to restrict to abelian sheaves). Taking 5.2 and 5.3 into account, the preceding formulas (5.4.1) and (5.4.2) give:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.5

Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a finite morphism of preschemes, \(y\) a point of \(Y\). Then for every sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), one has an isomorphism (functorial in \(F\)) \[ f_*(F)_{\bar{y}} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \prod_{x \in X_y \otimes_{k(y)} k(\bar{y})} F_{\bar{x}} , \] (consequently the formation of \(f_*(F)\) commutes with every base change \(Y' \to Y\)), and if \(F\) is an abelian sheaf, one has \[ R^q f_*(F) = 0 \quad \text{if } q > 0 . \]

Note that the first formula of 5.5 is in fact independent of 5.2 and of the general passage-to-the-limit theorem VII 5.7, and that it implies (thanks to 3.5) that \(F \mapsto f_*(F)\) is an exact functor on the category of abelian sheaves, whence again \(R^q f_*(F) = 0\) for \(q \neq 0\). Here is a slight variant of 5.5:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.6

Let \(f : X \to Y\) be an integral morphism. Then for every abelian sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), we have \[ R^q f_*(F) = 0 \quad \text{for } q \neq 0 . \] Moreover, the functor \(f_*\) on sheaves of sets commutes with every base change \(Y' \to Y\).

Indeed, by 5.2 we are reduced to proving that when \(Y\) is strictly local, we have \(H^q(X,F) = 0\) for every abelian sheaf on \(X\). Now we will have \(Y = \operatorname{Spec} A\), \(X = \operatorname{Spec} B\), with \(B\) an integral algebra, and writing \(B = \varinjlim B_i\), where \(B_i\) ranges over the subalgebras of finite type of \(B\) (which are even finite over \(A\)), we will have \(X = \varprojlim_i X_i\), where \(X_i = \operatorname{Spec} B_i\). By VII 5.13, we are reduced to proving that \(R^q f_*(F_i) = 0\) for \(q \neq 0\), \(F_i\) an abelian sheaf on \(X_i\), which follows from 5.5. The last assertion of 5.6 is proved by the same method of reduction to 5.5.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.7

Let \(f : X \to Y\) be an immersion morphism. Then for every sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the canonical morphism \[ f^* f_*(F) \to F \] is an isomorphism.

Since \(f\) factors as the composite of an open immersion and a closed immersion, and since 5.7 is trivial in the case of an open immersion (IV n° 3), we are reduced to the case where \(f\) is a closed immersion. We are reduced to proving that for every \(x \in X\), the corresponding homomorphism \[ (f^* f_*(F))_{\bar{x}} \to F_{\bar{x}} \] is bijective; now by transitivity of stalks (3.4) the first term is none other than the stalk \(f_*(F)_{\bar{x}}\), so we must verify that the canonical homomorphism \[ f_*(F)_{\bar{x}} \to F_{\bar{x}} \] is bijective, which follows immediately from 5.5.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.8

Using 5.5 and proceeding again as in 5.6, one easily proves that if \(f : X \to Y\) is an integral morphism, \(F\) a sheaf of groups on \(X\) (not necessarily commutative), then \(R^1 f_*(F)\) is the final sheaf on \(Y\) (compare remark 5.3).
6. Supports

Let \(U\) be a Zariski open of the scheme \(X\). Then \(U \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}}\), and in fact \(U\) is a subobject of the final object \(X\) of \(X_{\text{ét}}\), hence defines a subobject \(\widetilde{U}\) of the final object of \(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\), i.e. an "open" of the étale topos \(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\) of \(X\) (IV 8.3).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.1

The preceding map \(U \mapsto \widetilde{U}\) is an isomorphism from the ordered set of opens (in the sense of Zariski) of \(X\), onto the set of opens of the étale topos \(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\).

Since \(X_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\) is fully faithful, we see immediately that the map \(U \mapsto \widetilde{U}\) preserves the order structures, i.e. \((U \subset V) \Leftrightarrow (\widetilde{U} \subset \widetilde{V})\); in particular the preceding map is injective. To prove that it is surjective, consider a subsheaf \(F\) of the final sheaf \(\widetilde{X}\), and consider the objects of \(X_{\text{ét}/F}\), i.e. the étale schemes \(X'\) over \(X\) such that \(F(X') \neq \varnothing\). Since \(X' \to X\) is étale, it is an open map (EGA IV 2.4.6); in particular its image (in the set-theoretic sense) \(\operatorname{Im}(X')\) is open. Let \(U\) be the open which is the union of the \(\operatorname{Im}(X')\) (\(X' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}/F}\)). Since the family of the \(X' \to U\) (\(X' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}/F}\)) is surjective, hence covering, we conclude that \(U \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}/F}\), hence \(X_{\text{ét}/F} = X_{\text{ét}/U}\), hence \(F = U\), qed.

In view of 6.1, we may therefore speak without ambiguity of an "open" of \(X\), without specifying whether we understand this notion in the usual sense of Zariski or in the sense of the étale topology.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.2

Let \(U\) be an open of \(X\), \(j : U \to X\) the canonical immersion; then the functor \[ j^* : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{U}_{\text{ét}} \] induces an equivalence of categories \[ \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}/\widetilde{U}} \to \widetilde{U}_{\text{ét}} . \]

Indeed, one verifies immediately that for every site \(C\) where finite \(\varprojlim\) exist, and for every subobject \(U\) of the final object \(e\) of \(C\), considering the functor \(j : C \to C_{/U}\) defined by \(j(S) = S \times U\), \(j\) is a morphism of sites and \(j^* : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C}_{/U}\) induces an equivalence \(\widetilde{C}_{/U} \to \widetilde{C}_{/U}\). It then suffices to combine this general fact with the fact that \(U_{\text{ét}}\) is canonically isomorphic to \(X_{\text{ét}/U}\).

Figuratively, one can express 6.2 by saying that the operations of "inducing on an open", in the usual sense for schemes on the one hand, and in the sense of topoi on the other, are compatible. Here is an analogous compatibility for the operations of "restriction to a closed subset":

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 6.3

Let \(X\) be a scheme, \(Y\) a closed subscheme of \(X\), \(U = X - Y\) endowed with the induced structure, \(i : Y \to X\) and \(j : U \to X\) the canonical immersions. Then the functor \[ i_* : \widetilde{Y}_{\text{ét}} \to \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \] is fully faithful, and if \(F \in \mathrm{Ob}\, \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\), \(F\) is isomorphic to a sheaf of the form \(i_*(G)\) iff \(j^*(F)\) is isomorphic to the final sheaf \(\widetilde{U}\) on \(U\).

Proof. Since \(i_*\) and \(i^*\) are adjoint to one another, the fact that \(i_*\) is fully faithful is also equivalent to the fact that the functorial homomorphism \[ i^*(i_*(G)) \to G \] is an isomorphism, which is none other than 5.7. On the other hand, if \(G \in \mathrm{Ob}\, \widetilde{Y}_{\text{ét}}\), then one verifies trivially by 6.2 that \(j^*(i_*(G))\) is the final sheaf on \(U\). Conversely, if \(F \in \mathrm{Ob}\, \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\) is such that \(j^*(F)\) is the final sheaf, let us prove that \(F\) is isomorphic to a sheaf of the form \(i_*(G)\), or what amounts to the same, that the canonical homomorphism \[ G \to i_* i^*G \] is an isomorphism. Now it suffices to verify once again that for every \(x \in X\), the homomorphism induced on the geometric stalks at \(\bar{x}\) is an isomorphism. When \(x \in U\), this is none other than the hypothesis made on \(G\). When \(x \in Y\), by transitivity of stalks we are reduced to verifying that the homomorphism on the stalks at \(\bar{x}\) induced by \[ i^*(G) \to i^*(i_*(i^*(G))) \] is an isomorphism; now the preceding homomorphism is an isomorphism by 5.7 applied to \(F = i^*G\) and to \(i\). This completes the proof of 6.3.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.4

The functor \(i_*\) induces an equivalence of the category of abelian sheaves on \(Y\) with the category of abelian sheaves on \(X\) whose restriction to \(U = X - Y\) is zero.
In accordance with common usage we shall therefore often identify an abelian sheaf on \(Y\) with an abelian sheaf on \(X\) that is zero on \(U\).

By 6.1 we thus know (if \(X\) is a scheme) how to interpret the "opens" of the topos \(E = \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\) as opens \(U\) of \(X\) in the usual sense, and by 6.3 with this identification the "residual topos" \(E_{\complement U}\) of IV 3 is canonically equivalent to the topos \(\widetilde{Y}_{\text{ét}}\), where \(Y = X - U\) is endowed with an arbitrary induced structure making \(Y\) a scheme. We can consequently apply to this situation the results of IV 3., in particular the description IV 3.3 of sheaves \(F\) on \(X\) in terms of triples \((F', F'', u)\) where \(F'\) is a sheaf on \(Y\), \(F''\) a sheaf on \(U\) and \(u\) a homomorphism of \(F'\) into \(i^*j_*(F'')\). We shall freely use in what follows the notations \(i^!\), \(j_!\) of IV.3, which denote functors \[ j_! : (\widetilde{U}_{\text{ét}})_{ab} \to (\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}})_{ab} , \] \[ i^! : (\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}})_{ab} \to (\widetilde{Y}_{\text{ét}})_{ab} , \] where the subscript "ab" denotes the category of abelian sheaves. These functors give rise to the two exact sequences IV 3.7.

In view of the foregoing developments and of the general terminology introduced in IV 8.5, it is appropriate to introduce, for an abelian sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), or a section \(\varphi\) of such a sheaf, the notion of support of \(F\) resp. of \(\varphi\), as being the closed set (in the usual sense, i.e. of Zariski) complementary to the largest open on which the object in question vanishes.

In the present situation, it is likewise imperative to replace the general notations V 4.3 \(H^q(E_{\complement U}, F)\), \(H^q_{\complement U}(F)\) by the notations \(H^q_Y(X,F)\), \(\underline{H}^q_Y(F)\), the first denoting an abelian group, the second a sheaf abelian on \(Y\) (or again an abelian sheaf on \(X\), zero on \(U\)). Thus, we have \(\underline{H}^q_Y = R^q i^!\) etc...
I refer to V 6 for the general properties of the preceding functors.
7. Specialization morphisms of stalk functors

We saw in N° 4 how one associates, to every geometric point \(\xi\) of the scheme \(X\), a strictly local \(X\)-scheme \[ \overline{X}(\xi) = \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,\xi} , \] depending, in fact, only on the geometric point above the image \(x\) of \(\xi\) defined by the separable closure \(\overline{k(x)}\) of \(k(x)\) in \(\Omega = k(\xi)\). We shall often restrict ourselves in what follows to the geometric points \(\xi = \operatorname{Spec} \Omega\) that are algebraic separable over \(X\), i.e. such that \(\Omega\) is a separable closure of \(k(x)\), i.e. \(\xi = \bar{x}\). Let us call an \(X\)-scheme \(Z\) a strict localization of \(X\) if it is \(X\)-isomorphic to a scheme of the form \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,\bar{x}}\); we thus see that \[ \xi \mapsto \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,\xi} = \overline{X}(\xi) \] is an equivalence from the category of geometric points that are algebraic separable over \(X\), with the category of \(X\)-schemes that are strict localizations of \(X\), when one takes as morphisms in both categories the isomorphisms alone.
This last statement is no longer exact when one takes as morphisms all the \(X\)-morphisms, for in the second category there may be \(X\)-morphisms that are not isomorphisms. One then poses the

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.2

Let \(\xi\), \(\xi'\) be two geometric points of the scheme \(X\); one calls specialization arrow from \(\xi'\) to \(\xi\) any \(X\)-morphism between the corresponding strict localizations \[ \overline{X}(\xi') \to \overline{X}(\xi) . \]
One says that \(\xi\) is a specialization of \(\xi'\) or that \(\xi'\) is a generization of \(\xi\), if there exists a specialization arrow from \(\xi'\) to \(\xi\).

One will note that specialization arrows compose in the evident way, so that taking as morphisms the specialization arrows, the geometric points of \(X\) form a category, equivalent (as does the full subcategory formed by the geometric points algebraic and separable over \(X\)) to the full subcategory of \((\mathrm{Sch})_{/X}\) formed by the strict localizations of \(X\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.3

Let \(X\) be a scheme, \(Z\) an \(X\)-scheme which is isomorphic to a pseudo-filtered projective limit of étale \(X\)-schemes \(X_i\), with affine transition morphisms (VII 5.1), \(\xi'\) a geometric point of \(X\), \(Z' = \overline{X}(\xi')\) the corresponding strict localization. Then:

a) The restriction map \[ \operatorname{Hom}_X(Z',Z) \to \operatorname{Hom}_X(\xi',Z) \] is bijective.

b) For both terms to be non-empty, it is necessary and sufficient that the image \(x'\) of \(\xi'\) in \(X\) lie in that of \(Z\).

c) Let \(T\) be a \(Z\)-scheme; for \(T\) to be a strict localization of \(Z\), it is necessary and sufficient that it be a strict localization of \(X\).

Proof. a) One is reduced immediately to the case where \(Z\) is one of the \(X_i\), i.e. where \(Z\) is étale over \(X\), and by the base change \(Z' \to X\) one may assume that \(Z' \simeq X\), whence the conclusion by 4.2 (ii). b) One notes that if \(x'\) is the image of a point \(z\) of \(Z\), then \(k(z)\) is necessarily a separable algebraic extension of \(k(x')\), hence there exists a \(k(x')\)-homomorphism of the latter into \(k(\xi')\), whence the conclusion.
c) The proof is an easy exercise left to the reader.
From 7.2 and 7.3 one concludes:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.4

Let \(\xi\), \(\xi'\) be two geometric points of the scheme \(X\). Then the restriction map defines a bijection from the set \(\operatorname{Hom}_X(\overline{X}(\xi'), \overline{X}(\xi))\) of specialization arrows from \(\xi'\) to \(\xi\), with the set of \(X\)-morphisms from \(\xi'\) to \(\overline{X}(\xi)\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.5

For \(\xi\) to be a specialization of \(\xi'\), it is necessary and sufficient that the same hold for the images \(x, x'\) of \(\xi\), \(\xi'\) in \(X\), i.e. that \(x\) belong to the closure of \(\{x'\}\).
Since \(\operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,\xi} \to \operatorname{Spec} \mathcal{O}_{X,x}\) is faithfully flat (4.4) it is surjective, and it therefore suffices to apply the second assertion of 7.3.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.6

For every scheme \(X\), let \(\operatorname{Pt}(X)\) be the category of geometric points over \(X\) (or again, of geometric points algebraic separable over \(X\)), the morphisms being the specialization arrows. Let then \(\xi\) be a geometric point of a scheme \(X\), \(\overline{X}(\xi)\) the strict localization corresponding, one then has an equivalence of categories \[ \operatorname{Pt}(\overline{X}(\xi)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \operatorname{Pt}(X)_{/\xi} , \] obtained by associating, to every geometric point \(\xi'\) of \(\overline{X}(\xi)\), the geometric point corresponding on \(X\), with the specialization morphism into \(\xi\) deduced from the structural morphism \(\xi' \to \overline{X}(\xi)\) by 7.4.

In other words, giving a generization \(\xi'\) of the geometric point \(\xi\) is essentially equivalent to giving a geometric point of \(\overline{X}(\xi)\). Let us note moreover that by 7.3 c), the corresponding homomorphism \(\overline{X}(\xi') \to \overline{X}(\xi)\) makes \(\overline{X}(\xi')\) the strict localization of \(\overline{X}(\xi)\), relative to \(\xi'\).

Let us now interpret, for every geometric point \(\xi\) of \(X\) and every sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the stalk \(F_\xi\) as being \(\Gamma(\overline{X}(\xi), \overline{F}(\xi))\), where \(\overline{F}(\xi)\) is the inverse image of \(F\) on \(\overline{X}(\xi)\) (4.8). Then we see that every specialization arrow \[ u : \xi' \to \xi \] induces a homomorphism, functorial in \(F\): \[ u^* : F_\xi \to F_{\xi'} , \] called the specialization homomorphism associated with the specialization arrow \(u\). It is evident, by the transitivity of inverse images of sheaves, that for a composed specialization arrow one has: \[ (wu)^* = u^* w^* . \]

If \(E\) is a topos, recall (IV ) that one has called "stalk functor", or (by abuse of language) "point" of the topos \(E\), any morphism from the "final topos" (Ens) (isomorphic to the category of sheaves on a space reduced to a point!) into \(E\), i.e. any functor \[ \varphi = E \to (\mathrm{Ens}) \] which commutes with arbitrary inductive limits, and with finite projective limits. It is appropriate to regard the set of stalk functors of \(E\) as the set of objects of a full subcategory of \(\operatorname{Hom}(E,(\mathrm{Ens}))\), called category of stalk functors of the topos \(E\), whose opposite is called category of points of \(E\), and denoted \(\operatorname{Pt}(E)\), cf. (IV 6.1).

When \(E\) is of the form \(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\), where \(X\) is a scheme, we defined in 3.3 and 7.7 a functor \[ (*) \qquad \operatorname{Pt}(X) \to \operatorname{Pt}(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}) , \] where the first term is defined in 7.6. This being posed, one has the

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 7.9

Let \(X\) be a scheme. The preceding functor \((*)\) is an equivalence from the category of geometric points on \(X\) (with as morphisms the specialization arrows) with the category of points of the étale topos \(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\) (opposite of that of the stalk functors on \(\widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\)).

Since this theorem will no longer be used in the sequel of the seminar, we confine ourselves here to a sketch of the proof, in which we shall allow ourselves certain liberties with questions of universe.

a) The functor under consideration is fully faithful. For every \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}}\), let \(\check{X} : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) be defined by \[ \check{X}(F) = \operatorname{Hom}(X,F) = F(X) . \] Note that the stalk functor \[ \mathscr{E}_\xi : F \mapsto F_\xi \] can be written \[ \mathscr{E}_\xi \simeq \varinjlim_i \check{X}_i , \] where the \(X_i\) are affine schemes étale over \(X\), indexed by a certain filtered category (cf. 4.3 and 4.5). One thus has for every functor \(\varphi : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to (\mathrm{Ens})\): \[ \operatorname{Hom}(\mathscr{E}_\xi, \varphi) \simeq \varprojlim_i \operatorname{Hom}(\check{X}_i, \varphi) , \] on the other hand it is well known that one has a bifunctorial isomorphism \[ \operatorname{Hom}(\check{X}_i, \varphi) \simeq \varphi(X_i) . \]

When \(\varphi\) is of the form \(\mathscr{E}_{\xi'}\), hence \[ \varphi \simeq \varinjlim_j \check{X}_j , \] one thus has a natural bijection \[ (*) \qquad \operatorname{Hom}(\mathscr{E}_\xi, \mathscr{E}_{\xi'}) \simeq \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_X(X'_j, X_i) . \] On the other hand one has (in the category of schemes) \[ \overline{X}(\xi) = \varprojlim_i X_i , \qquad \overline{X}(\xi') = \varprojlim_j X'_j , \] whence \[ \operatorname{Hom}_X(\overline{X}(\xi'), \overline{X}(\xi)) \simeq \varprojlim_i \operatorname{Hom}_X(\overline{X}(\xi'), X_i) , \] on the other hand, since \(X_i\) is locally of finite presentation over \(X\), one has \[ \operatorname{Hom}_X(\overline{X}(\xi'), X_i) \simeq \varinjlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_X(X'_j, X_i) , \] whence \[ (**) \qquad \operatorname{Hom}_X(\overline{X}(\xi'), \overline{X}(\xi)) \simeq \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \operatorname{Hom}_X(X'_j, X_i) . \] The comparison of \((*)\) and \((**)\) gives the desired conclusion (up to a verification of compatibilities, left to the reader).
b) The functor under consideration is essentially surjective.

Let us first remark that if \(C\) is a site where finite \(\varprojlim\) are representable, \(\widetilde{C} = E\) the corresponding topos, then every stalk functor \(\varphi\) on \(E\) can be represented as a "filtered inductive limit" of functors of the form \[ \check{Y}(F) = F(\widetilde{Y}) = \operatorname{Hom}(\widetilde{Y}, F), \qquad Y \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C , \] (where \(\widetilde{Y}\) is the sheaf associated with \(Y\)), in the following way (∗). One considers the category \(C_{/\varphi}\) of pairs \((Y, \xi)\), with \(Y \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\), \(\xi \in \varphi(\widetilde{Y})\) (the morphisms being defined in the evident way), and one notes that one has an evident homomorphism \[ (*) \qquad \varinjlim_{(Y,\xi) \in C_{/\varphi}} \check{Y} \to \varphi \] by remarking that \[ \operatorname{Hom}(\varinjlim_{C_{/\varphi}} \check{Y}, \varphi) \simeq \varprojlim_{C_{/\varphi}} \operatorname{Hom}(\check{Y}, \varphi) \simeq \varprojlim_{C_{/\varphi}} \varphi(\widetilde{Y}) . \] Now one has a canonical element in \(\varprojlim_{C_{/\varphi}} \varphi(\widetilde{Y})\), by associating to every \((Y, \xi)\) the element \(\xi\) of \(\varphi(\widetilde{Y})\). Using the fact that finite \(\varprojlim\) exist in \(C\), and that the functor \(Y \mapsto \varphi(\widetilde{Y})\) commutes with them, we see that in \(C_{/\varphi}\) the finite \(\varprojlim\) exist; a fortiori \(C_{/\varphi}\) is filtered. Using that every sheaf \(F\) is an inductive limit of sheaves of the form \(\widetilde{Y}\), and using the fact that \(\varphi\) commutes with inductive limits, one easily concludes that the homomorphism of functors \((*)\) is bijective, and thus gives the announced representation.

Let us also remark that if \(E\) is a topos, \(Y\) an object of \(E\), whence a topos \(E_{/Y}\), then giving a stalk functor \(\varphi\) for \(E_{/Y}\) is equivalent to giving a pair \((\varphi, \xi)\), where \(\varphi\) is a stalk functor for \(E\), and \(\xi \in \varphi(Y)\). To the stalk functor \(\psi : E_{/Y} \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) one associates the pair \((\varphi, \xi)\), where \(\varphi\) is the composite \(Z \mapsto \varphi(Z) = \psi(Z \times Y)\), and where \(\xi \in \varphi(Y) = \psi(Y \times Y)\) is the image of the unique element of \(\psi(Y)\) by the diagonal morphism of \(Y \times Y\).

Let us now return to the case of the site \(C = X_{\text{ét}}\), and let \(\varphi : \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}} \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) be a stalk functor on the étale topos of \(X\). Considering the restriction of \(\varphi\) to the full subcategory of \(X_{\text{ét}}\) formed by the opens of this topos, or what amounts to the same (6.1) by the opens \(U\) of \(X\), one finds a map \[ \varphi_o : \mathcal{U}(X) \to \{0, 1\} \] commuting with arbitrary sups and finite infs. (One notes that for \(U \in \mathcal{U}(X)\), \(\varphi(U)\) is empty or reduced to a point, and one takes \(\varphi_o(U) = 0\) or 1 according as one is in the one or the other case).

One sees easily, thanks to the fact that every irreducible closed set of \(X\) has a unique generic point(∗), that \(\varphi_o\) is defined by means of a unique \(x \in X\), by the condition \[ \varphi_o(U) = 1 \quad \text{iff} \quad x \in U , \] i.e. \[ \varphi(U) \neq \varnothing \Longleftrightarrow x \in U . \] Let \(F \in \mathrm{Ob}\, \widetilde{X}_{\text{ét}}\); then the image of \(F\) in the final sheaf \(\widetilde{X}\) is an open; and since \[ \varphi(F) \to \varphi(U) \] is surjective, we see that \(\varphi(F) \neq \varnothing\) iff \(\varphi(U) \neq \varnothing\), i.e. iff \(x \in U\). Let then \(C_{/\varphi}\) be the category of pairs \((X', \xi)\) where \(X' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}}\), and \(\xi \in \varphi(X')\). It was noted in 7.9.1 that \(C_{/\varphi}\) is filtered connected. Moreover, thanks to 7.9.2 and to what precedes applied to \(X'\) instead of \(X\), if \((X', \xi) \in \mathrm{Ob}\, X_{\text{ét}}\), there is associated with it a unique point \(x' \in X'\), such that for an étale morphism \(X'' \to X'\), \(\xi\) is in the image of \(\varphi(X'') \to \varphi(X')\) iff \(x'\) is in that of \(X''\). One concludes from this that the scheme \(\varprojlim\) of the \(X'\) along the category \(C\) of the \((X', \xi)\) exists and is a strict localization \(Z\) of \(X\), thus corresponding to a geometric point \(\xi\) and a stalk functor \(\mathscr{E}_\xi\).

For every sheaf \(F\), one then has \[ \mathscr{E}_\xi(F) \simeq \varinjlim_{C_\varphi} F(X') . \] In view of 7.9.1 one concludes that \(\varphi\) is isomorphic to \(\mathscr{E}_\xi\), which completes the proof of 7.9.

pages.title: 8. Two spectral sequences for integral morphisms

blocks.html: 8. Two spectral sequences for integral morphisms

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.1

Let \(f : X \to Y\) be a surjective integral morphism, \(F\) an abelian sheaf on \(Y\). For every integer \(i\), let \(\mathscr{H}^i(F)\) be the presheaf on \((\mathrm{Sch})_{/Y}\) defined by \[ \mathscr{H}^i(F)(Z) = H^i(Z, F_Z) , \] where \(F_Z\) is the inverse image of \(F\) on \(Z\). Then there exists a spectral sequence (functorial in \(F\)) \[ H^*(X,F) \Longleftarrow E_2^{pq} = H^p(X/Y, \mathscr{H}^q(F)) \] ("descent spectral sequence").

Of course, the symbol \(H^p(X/Y, G)\), for a presheaf \(G\) on \((\mathrm{Sch})_{/Y}\), denotes the \(p\)-th relative Čech cohomology group, defined by means of the complex of the \(C^n(X/Y,G) = G(X^{n+1})\), where \(X^m\) denotes the \(m\)-th power in \((\mathrm{Sch})_{/Y}\). To establish 8.1, let \(p_n : X^{n+1} \to Y\) be the projection, and set \[ A^n = p_{n*}(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{X^{n+1}}) , \] where \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{X^{n+1}}\) denotes the constant sheaf \(\mathbf{Z}\) on \(X^{n+1}\). Then the \(A^n\) are the components of a simplicial abelian sheaf on \(Y\), hence of a complex of abelian sheaves \(A^*\) on \(Y\). Note that one has an evident homomorphism \[ (*) \qquad \underline{\mathbf{Z}}_Y \to A^0 . \] This being posed, one has the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.2

The complex \((A^*)\) endowed with the homomorphism \((*)\) is a resolution of \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_Y\). More generally, for every abelian sheaf \(F\) on \(Y\), \(A^* \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} F\) is a resolution of \(F\).

Proof: One may assume \(Y\) affine, hence \(Y = \operatorname{Spec} A\), \(X = \operatorname{Spec} B\), where \(B\) is an integral \(A\)-algebra. One will have \(B = \varinjlim_i B_i\), where \(B_i\) ranges over the subalgebras of finite type, hence finite, of \(B\), whence \(X = \varprojlim_i X_i\), where \(X_i = \operatorname{Spec} B_i\). Using VII 5.11, one sees that the augmented complex \(A^*(X/Y)\) is then the inductive limit of the augmented complexes \(A^*(X_i/Y)\). This reduces us to the case where \(f\) is finite. It suffices to prove that for every geometric point \(\bar{y}\) of \(Y\), the complex \(A^*_{\bar{y}}\) is a resolution of \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{\bar{y}}\), and remains so after tensoring by an \(F\). But if \(X_{\bar{y}}\) is the fibre of \(X\) at \(\bar{y}\), it follows from 5.5 that the complex \(A^*_{\bar{y}}\) is none other than the analogous complex \(A^*(X_{\bar{y}}/\bar{y})\). This reduces us to the case where \(Y\) is the spectrum of a separably closed field \(k\). Using 1.3 a) and b), one may even assume \(k\) algebraically closed, and \(X\) reduced, hence \(X\) of the form \(I_Y\), where \(I\) is a finite set. But then the complex \(A^* \otimes F\) identifies with the trivial cochain complex of the index set \(I\) with coefficients in \(F_{\bar{y}}\), hence it is indeed a resolution of \(F_{\bar{y}}\).

We thus obtain, as a consequence of 8.2, a spectral sequence \[ H^*(Y,F) \Longleftarrow E_2^{pq} = H^p(H^q(Y, A^* \otimes F)) , \] and it remains to make explicit the initial term. Now one has a canonical homomorphism \[ A^n \otimes F \to p_{n*} p_n^*(F) , \] and the latter is an isomorphism, as one sees again by reduction to the case \(f\) finite and passage to the fibres. Using 5.5, one concludes \[ H^q(Y, A^n \otimes F) \simeq H^q(X^{n+1}, p_n^*(F)) = \mathscr{H}^q(F)(X^{n+1}), \] which indeed gives the initial term announced in 8.1.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 8.3

a) When one is given a locally finite covering of \(Y\) by closed sets \(Y_i\), and one sets \(X = \coprod_i Y_i\) then the canonical morphism \(f : X \to Y\) is finite, and the spectral sequence 8.1 has an initial term which is made explicit as the cohomology of the complex defined by the \(H^q(Y_{i_0 \ldots i_p}, F|Y_{i_0 \ldots i_p})\), where \(Y_{i_0 \ldots i_p} = Y_{i_0} \cap \ldots \cap Y_{i_p}\). It is thus the analogue of the Leray spectral sequence for a locally finite closed covering of an ordinary topological space (TF Chapter II 5.2.4). The latter can moreover be generalized likewise to a spectral sequence relative to a "finite" morphism i.e. proper with finite fibres, by proceeding as in 8.1.

b) One will note the analogy of the spectral sequence of 8.1 with the Leray spectral sequence of a covering \((X_i)\) of \(Y\) (in this case by \(X_i\) étale over \(Y\)); the latter would be obtained formally by writing the spectral sequence 8.1 for \(X = \coprod_i X_i\). It is in fact probable that these two spectral sequences admit a common generalization, which would be valid whenever one had a family of morphisms \((X_i \to Y)\), which is a "family of universal effective descent" for the fibred category of étale sheaves on a variable base scheme (cf n° 9 below). The analogous question is moreover posed in ordinary topology, concerning a common generalization of the two kinds of Leray spectral sequences of a covering, assumed either open, or locally finite closed (∗).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.4

Let \(Y\) be a scheme, \(\pi\) a profinite group, \((\pi_i)_i\) the projective system of the finite discrete quotient groups of \(\pi\), \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) a projective system of principal coverings of \(Y\), with groups the \(\pi_i\), the transition homomorphisms \(X_j \to X_i\) being compatible with the homomorphisms \(\pi_j \to \pi_i\) on the groups of operators, \(X = \varprojlim X_i\) (cf. VII 5.1), so that the group \(\pi\) operates on the \(Y\)-scheme \(X\), \(F\) an abelian sheaf on \(Y\). Then one has a "Hochschild-Serre" spectral sequence (functorial in \(F\)) \[ H^*(Y,F) \Longleftarrow E_2^{pq} = H^p(\pi, \varinjlim_i H^q(X_i, F_{X_i})) , \] where \(F_{X_i}\) is the inverse image of \(F\) on \(X_i\), and \(H^p(\pi, -)\) denotes Galois cohomology.

The term \(E_2^{pq}\) written here is also (by definition of \(H^p(\pi, -)\) and transitivity of inductive limits) isomorphic to \[ E_2^{pq} = \varinjlim_i H^p(\pi_i, H^q(X_i, F_{X_i})) , \] which shows us that it suffices to find an inductive system of spectral sequences (depending on the index \(i\)) \[ H^*(Y, F) \Longleftarrow {}^i E_2^{pq} = H^p(\pi_i, H^q(X_i, F_{X_i})) . \] This reduces us to defining the spectral sequence in the case where \(\pi\) is finite. Then \(f : X \to Y\) is a covering morphism in \(Y_{\text{ét}}\), so one can write the Leray spectral sequence of this morphism. In view of the canonical isomorphisms: \[ X^n \simeq X \times_\pi G^n , \] a well-known computation then shows that for every presheaf \(\mathscr{H}\) on \(X_{\text{ét}}\), transforming sums into products, \(C^*(X/Y, \mathscr{H})\) is none other than the complex of homogeneous cochains of \(G\) with coefficients in \(\mathscr{H}(X)\), whence the announced form for the initial term.

A variant of this proof, avoiding all computation, consists in regarding \(E \mapsto X \times_\pi E\) as a morphism from the site of finite \(\pi\)-sets into the étale site of \(Y\), and in writing the spectral sequence of Leray of this morphism. Finally, when \(\pi\) is finite, one can also regard the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence as being a special case of 8.1 relative to the morphism \(f : X \to Y\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.5

Suppose \(Y\) quasi-compact and quasi-separated; then the spectral sequence of 8.4 is written \[ H^*(Y,F) \Longleftarrow E_2^{pq} = H^p(\pi, H^q(X,F_X)) . \]
Indeed, by VII 5.8, one then has canonical isomorphisms \[ \varinjlim_i H^q(X_i, F_{X_i}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^q(X, F_X) . \]

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.6

Let \(Y\) be a henselian local scheme with closed point \(y\), \(F\) an abelian sheaf on \(Y\), \(F_o\) the sheaf induced on \(Y_o = \operatorname{Spec}(k(y))\). Then the canonical homomorphisms \[ H^n(Y,F) \to H^n(Y_o, F_o) \] are isomorphisms.

Let indeed \(\bar{y}\) be a geometric point over \(y\), corresponding to a separable closure \(\overline{k(y)} = k(\bar{y})\) of \(k(y)\); since \(Y\) is henselian, the strict localization \(X\) of \(Y\) at \(\bar{y}\) is the projective limit of the connected Galois étale \(\bar{y}\)-pointed coverings \(X_i\), so that we are under the conditions of application of 8.5. Since \(H^q(X, F_X) = 0\) for \(q > 0\) by 4.7, we conclude that there are isomorphisms \[ H^n(Y,F) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } H^n(\pi, F(X)) , \] where \(\pi\) is the "Galois group" of \(X\) over \(Y\), isomorphic to that of \(\overline{k(y)}\) over \(k = k(y)\). One finds similarly (or by 2.3) \[ H^n(Y_o, F_o) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } H^n(\pi, F_o(X_o)) , \] where \(X_o = X \times_Y Y_o \simeq \operatorname{Spec}(\overline{k(y)})\). Now the restriction homomorphism \(F(X) \to F_o(X_o)\) is an isomorphism by 4.8, whence the conclusion 8.6 follows immediately.

footnotes.html: (∗) Since the writing of these lines, P.Deligne has made a general theory of "descent spectral sequences", cf. Exp. Vbis.

blocks.html: 9. Descent of étale sheaves
The present number will no longer be used in the sequel of this Seminar, and may be omitted on a first reading.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 9.1

Let \(f : X' \to X\) be a surjective (resp. universally submersive (SGA 1 IX 2.1)) morphism of schemes. Then the functor \[ f^* : X_{\text{ét}} \to X'_{\text{ét}} \] is faithful and "conservative" (cf. 3.6) (resp. induces a fully faithful functor from the category of sheaves on \(X_{\text{ét}}\) into the category of sheaves on \(X'_{\text{ét}}\) endowed with a descent datum relative to \(f : X' \to X\)).

The first point follows immediately from the transitivity of stalk functors (3.4) and from (3.7), the second (which is also stated by saying that \(f\) is a descent morphism relative to the fibred category of étale sheaves on variable schemes) also means that for two sheaves \(F, G\) on \(Y\), the natural diagram \[ (*) \qquad \operatorname{Hom}(F, G) \to \operatorname{Hom}(F', G') \rightrightarrows \operatorname{Hom}(F'', G'') \] is exact, where \(F'\) and \(G'\) (resp. \(F''\) and \(G''\)) are the inverse images of \(F\) and \(G\) on \(X'\) (resp. on \(X'' = X' \times_X X'\)). Taking for \(F\) the final sheaf, the statement gives the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.2

Let \(f : X' \to X\) be a universally submersive morphism. Then for every sheaf \(F\) on \(X\), the diagram \[ \Gamma(X, F) \to \Gamma(X', F') \rightrightarrows \Gamma(X'', F'') \] is exact, where \(X'' = X' \times_X X'\), and where \(F', F''\) are the inverse images of \(F\) on \(X'\), \(X''\).
We shall prove 9.1 using the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.3

Suppose \(f\) universally submersive. Let \(F\) be a sheaf on \(X\); denote by \(S(F)\) the set of subsheaves of \(X\), and define analogously \(S(F')\), \(S(F'')\). Then the diagram of natural maps \[ S(F) \to S(F') \rightrightarrows S(F'') \] is exact.

Proof. The fact that \(S(F) \to S(F')\) is injective follows immediately from the fact that the functor \(f^*\) is conservative; for if \(F_i\) (\(i = 1, 2\)) are two subsheaves of \(F\) such that \(f^*(F_1) = f^*(F_2)\), then the inclusions \(F_3 = F_1 \cap F_2 \to F_i\) (\(i = 1, 2\)) are isomorphisms, since they become such after application of the functor \(f^*\), hence \(F_1 = F_2\). It remains to prove that if \(G'\) is a subsheaf of \(F'\) such that \(\mathrm{pr}_1^*(G') = \mathrm{pr}_2^*(G')\), then \(G'\) is the inverse image of a subsheaf of \(F\). Note that one can find an epimorphism \(F_1 \to F\) in \(X_{\text{ét}}\), where \(F_1\) is representable by a scheme étale over \(X\). Let us introduce \(F_2 = F_1 \times_F F_1\), and likewise \(F'_1\), \(F''_1\), \(F'_2\), \(F''_2\), sheaves giving rise to a diagram of sets \[ \xymatrix{ S(F) \ar[r] \ar[d] & S(F') \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] \ar[d] & S(F'') \ar[d] \\ S(F_1) \ar[r] \ar@<0.5ex>[d] \ar@<-0.5ex>[d] & S(F'_1) \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] \ar@<0.5ex>[d] \ar@<-0.5ex>[d] & S(F''_1) \ar@<0.5ex>[d] \ar@<-0.5ex>[d] \\ S(F_2) \ar[r] & S(F'_2) \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] & S(F''_2) } \] in which the columns are exact, thanks to the exactness properties in the category of sheaves on \(X, X', X''\) respectively. A standard diagram-chasing then shows that, to prove that the first row is exact, it suffices to prove it for rows 2 and 3. Now for row 2 this follows from the fact that \(F_1\) is representable, \(X' \to X\) universally submersive, and from SGA IX 2.3. On the other hand, \(F_2\) is also representable, since it is a subsheaf of \(F_1 \times_X F_1\) which is representable, and one applies 6.1. Hence row 3 is also exact, qed.

Let us now prove 9.1, i.e. that every morphism \(u' : F' \to G'\), compatible with the descent data on \(F', G'\), \(u'\) comes from a morphism \(u : F \to G\). Let \(H = F \times G\), hence \(H' = F' \times G'\), \(H'' = F'' \times G''\); then the graph of \(u'\) is a subsheaf \(\Gamma'\) of \(H'\), whose two inverse images are equal to the graph of one and the same morphism \(u'' : F'' \to G''\). Hence by 9.3, \(\Gamma'\) comes from a subsheaf \(\Gamma\) of \(H\). I claim that \(\Gamma\) is the graph of a morphism \(u : F \to G\), i.e. that the morphism \(p : \Gamma \to F\) induced by \(\mathrm{pr}_1\) is an isomorphism: indeed, it becomes an isomorphism after the base change \(X' \to X\), and one applies the already proved part of 9.1. The morphism \(u : F \to G\) then answers the question, qed.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 9.4

Let \(f : X' \to X\) be a surjective morphism of schemes. Suppose that one of the following hypotheses is satisfied:

a) \(f\) is integral.

b) \(f\) is proper.

c) \(f\) is flat and locally of finite presentation (∗).

d) \(X\) is discrete (e.g. the spectrum of a field).

Then \(f\) is a morphism of effective descent for the fibred category \(\mathscr{F}\) on \((\mathrm{Sch})\) of étale sheaves on variable schemes, i.e. the functor \(f^*\) induces an equivalence of the category of sheaves on \(X\) with the category of sheaves on \(X'\), endowed with a descent datum relative to \(f : X' \to X\).

Let \(F'\) be a sheaf on \(X'\), endowed with a descent datum relative to \(f : X' \to X\). One then defines a functor \[ G : X_{\text{ét}}^o \to (\mathrm{Ens}) \] by the formula \[ G(Y) = \operatorname{Ker}(F'(Y') \rightrightarrows F''(Y'')) . \] One notes immediately that \(G\) is a sheaf for the étale topology; on the other hand one has a canonical injective homomorphism \(G \to f_*(F')\), whence a homomorphism \(f^*(G) \to F'\), and the latter is evidently compatible with the descent data. It remains to examine whether this homomorphism is an isomorphism. Note that \(G\) is also definable by the exactness of \[ G \to f_*(F') \rightrightarrows g_*(F'') , \] hence for every base change \(Y \xrightarrow{\ h\ } X\) which commutes with the formation of \(f_*(F')\) and \(g_*(F'')\), \(h^*(G) = G_Y\) identifies with the "descended" sheaf of \(F'_Y\), by \(Y' \to Y\), and of course the homomorphism \(f_Y^*(G_Y) \to (F_Y)'\) is that deduced from \(f^*(G) \to F'\) by base change. Now suppose that the base change \(f : Y = X' \to X\) commutes with the formation of \(f_*(F')\) and \(g_*(F'')\), and note that since \(Y' = X' \times_X X'\) has a section over \(Y' = X'\), hence \(Y' \to Y\) is a morphism of effective descent for every fibred category, in particular for \(\mathscr{F}\), it follows that \(f_Y^*(G_Y) \to (F_Y)'\) is an isomorphism, hence \(f^*(G) \to F'\) becomes an isomorphism after the base change \(Y' = X' \times_X X' \to X'\). Since the latter has a section, \(f^*(G) \to F'\) is an isomorphism, hence the descent datum under consideration on \(F'\) is effective.

This proves theorem 9.4 in case a), thanks to 5.6. Case b) also follows from the fact that if \(f\) is proper, then \(f_*\) commutes with every base change \(Y' \to Y\), (which will be proved in a later exposé (XII 5.1 (i))).

In case c), the question being local on \(X\) one may assume \(X\) affine, and that there exists an affine scheme \(X'_1\), of finite presentation, quasi-finite and faithfully flat over \(X\), and an \(X\)-morphism \(X'_1 \to X'\), which reduces us to the case where \(f\) is quasi-finite. Localizing further on \(X\), in the sense of the étale topology this time, one sees that there will exist an open \(X'_1\) of \(X'\) such that \(X'_1 \to X\) is finite and surjective, which reduces us to the case where \(f\) is finite and surjective, already treated in a).

In case d), one may assume (by localizing on \(X\)) that \(X\) is reduced to a single point, and even, in view of 1.1, that it is the spectrum of a field \(k\). Moreover, \(f\) is universally open (EGA IV 2.4.9) hence we are under the conditions of 9.1, and the reasoning of 9.4.1 applies again, taking a base change with \(Y = \operatorname{Spec} k\), where \(k=k(x)\), for some \(x \in X\). But then it is still true that \(f_*\) commutes with the base change \(Y \to X\), as we shall see later (XVI 1.4 and 1.5).
This completes the proof of 9.4.
